1 Introduction

[Write in your own words: the problem (who wrote a digit, and are two digits by the same person), why it matters (e.g. forensic document examination, signature verification (Bromley et al. 1993)), the two approaches compared (a CNN classifier and a Siamese network), and a one-paragraph preview of the main findings.]

All code is in the accompanying bundle: src/ holds the modules, run_experiments.py trains every model and saves results to results/, and this report reads those results. The analysis was done in Python with Keras 3 on TensorFlow.

2 Data and exploratory analysis (Task 1)

[Describe the visible sources of variation: between writers (size, slant, aspect ratio, stroke weight, letter forms such as the hooked 1), between sessions (e.g. writer 3’s digit 1 in session 1 vs later sessions), and within a session (replicates nearly identical).]

Median distances are 2.7 (same writer, same session), 7.3 (same writer, different session) and 8.7 (different writers). Once writer and digit are known, adding the session raises the explained pixel variance from 0.475 to 0.914.

[Interpret: what these numbers say about the size of the session effect relative to writer differences, and why the near-duplicate replicates matter for evaluation (link forward to the evaluation design).]

Limitations of the simulated data. [Your list: e.g. only digits 0–4 and 20 writers; perfectly balanced; clean, centred, noise-free images with stamped strokes; session effects that look like simple parametric shifts; unknown generator settings, so models may learn the simulator’s rules rather than handwriting traits; effective sample size closer to the 500 writer × digit × session cells than to 25,000 images.]

3 Evaluation design and leakage (Task 4)

[Justify the choices in Table 3, explain what each test represents in practice, and discuss leakage and optimism. Points to cover: random splits put near-duplicate replicates in train and test (Table 4); writers cannot be held out for closed-set identification; validation data are reused for early stopping, thresholds and tuning; the decision to add augmentation was made after seeing session-5 accuracy (mild test reuse); only 4 test writers per fold; simulated data.]

4 Writer identification with a CNN (Task 2)

Prediction task. The input is a single 28 × 28 image, scaled to \([0,1]\); the response is the writer ID (20 classes). The digit is not given to the model. The CNN follows the Lecture 4 pattern (Table 5), is trained with categorical cross-entropy and Adam (batch size 128), and stops early when validation loss has not improved for 5 epochs. A second version adds random rotation (up to about 15°), zoom and shift (up to 10%) to the training images.

[Report and interpret: overall accuracy 0.635 (vs chance 0.05); overfitting of the baseline and the effect of augmentation (Figure 4); differences by digit and by writer; what accuracy, top-3 accuracy, macro F1 and the multi-image results mean in real-world terms (e.g. a shortlist for a human examiner; more handwriting gives more reliable attribution); the closed-set limitation (an unknown writer is always assigned to one of the 20).]

5 Siamese network for writer matching (Task 3)

Design. A shared embedding CNN (same convolutional layers as Table 5, then dense 128 and a 64-unit output scaled to length 1) maps each image to a vector. Training uses the triplet loss (Schroff et al. 2015), following the Keras example in the course notes (Essam and Valdarrama 2021): \[ L(A,P,N) = \max\!\left(\lVert f(A)-f(P)\rVert^2 - \lVert f(A)-f(N)\rVert^2 + \alpha,\ 0\right), \qquad \alpha = 0.5 . \] Two images are declared to be by the same writer when the squared distance between their embeddings is below a threshold chosen on validation writers (src/siamese.py).

[Explain why the digit is held fixed in every triplet and why positives come from a different session (link to the EDA).]

As a comparison, a second Siamese network with contrastive loss (Hadsell et al. 2006) was implemented by Lehlonono Nkejane (originally in R; ported to Python in src/contrastive.py): a smaller encoder (16-dimensional embedding), one fixed set of 6,000 training pairs (same digit, different sessions, half same-writer), 10 epochs. Both models are evaluated on the same test pairs.

[Explain how matching performance is evaluated (AUC, equal error rate, false accept and false reject rates at a validation-chosen threshold) and what each means in practice. Interpret: performance on unseen writers vs raw pixels; triplet vs contrastive (similar AUC, contrastive much faster to train); the spread across folds; by-digit differences; same-session vs different-session vs different-digit pairs (Table 4 and appendix Table 19).]

6 Hyperparameter sensitivity (Task 5)

The triplet margin (0.2, 0.5, 1.0) and the embedding size (16, 64) were varied for the Siamese network, trained on sessions 1–3 of all writers and scored on session 4 only. The default (0.5, 64) was repeated with three seeds to measure run-to-run variation.

Across the grid, validation AUC ranges from 0.934 to 0.948; the three seeds of the default setting range from 0.943 to 0.949. Identification accuracy ranges from 0.552 to 0.608 across the grid.

[Interpret: how sensitive each measure is relative to seed noise; which setting was chosen and why the choice is partly chance; limits of the search.]

7 Comparison of the CNN and the Siamese network (Task 6)

Both models are compared on the session split (test = session 5). The Siamese network identifies writers by the nearest prototype, the average embedding of each writer × digit in sessions 1–3 (Snell et al. 2017; Utkin et al. 2019); the CNN’s 128-unit feature layer is also used in the same way. For verification, a session-5 image is compared with a session 1–3 image of the same digit.

Spearman correlation between session shift and accuracy over the 20 writers: -0.39 for the CNN (p = 0.086) and -0.52 for the Siamese network (p = 0.019). Identification accuracy on session 4 / session 5 is 0.592 / 0.635 for the CNN and 0.627 / 0.663 for the Siamese network.

[Discuss critically: which model suits which task (closed-set identification vs open-set verification; enrolling a new writer without retraining); whether CNN features transfer to verification; which digits carry more writer information, how consistent the ranking is (Table 16) and how large differences are relative to noise (about ±0.015 for 1,000 images); how session changes affect performance (same- vs different-session pairs, session 4 vs 5, per-writer shift in Figure 8, writers that fail completely). Note that the chosen Siamese model is the best of three seeds on validation, which slightly favours it.]
